doc.title: George Masso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

chapter: Goodman, Hackett and the World's Greatest Jazz Band
title: Bobby Hackett persuades him to leave teaching
summary: Hackett, a friend of his father, urged him to leave security; a week in Raleigh led to a year's leave and the Goodman Sextet.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Yeah. Well you were convinced to come out of education into performing. I think I read this.

This is a great story I think. Bobby Hackett was a good friend and he was a friend of my dad’s. My father was a trumpet player, a professional trumpet player. And when I started playing, Bobby was from Providence originally, and I grew up in the Providence area. When Bobby would come into town, they would have me play with them sometimes, lots of times, just Bobby and I and a rhythm section. And at that time I was teaching school, I was raising four children, I was very much into the education bit. And Bobby would always say to me, “Maestro, when are you going to give up all that security and come out and scuffle with the rest of us?” And he got me to do it. He got me to take a leave of absence for one week one time.

Just get away for a week, and go to Raleigh, North Carolina with him and play with a quintet. It was so good that I put in for a year’s leave of absence. I got it. Through Bobby’s help, I went with the Benny Goodman Sextet, and then later on with the World’s Greatest Jazz Band, and I just never went back to teaching because it was a whole new career development.
You were at the college then?
At the University of Connecticut then, yes.
